summary: Kole Jain redesigns nine common UI elements (a mobile tab bar, a chart, UI cards, pricing cards, stickers, a sign-up modal, a footer, chips and an image carousel), fixing both how they look and how they work. Most fixes are small, concrete moves: line up the tab bar's add button with the other icons and give every tab an active state, stop curving chart lines, make a repeated card the link instead of adding a button, put form labels above inputs, and keep a footer simple when a site only has a handful of links. He also gives a few exact recipes, such as chip vertical padding at half or a quarter of the horizontal padding, a 4 px grid for sign-up and login modals, and an input style with an off-white fill and a 40% opacity stroke. For a design system, the video supplies component-level defaults and rules (tab bar, chart, card, pricing card, form field, footer, chip, carousel) and several either-or choices that can be shown as visual samples.
key_ideas: Elements copied from Dribbble often look good but fail on usability; each element needs both its UI and its UX checked.
A tab bar's raised, circled add button draws attention to the tab people use least; drop it into line with the other icons.
Color is only useful if it can be seen: inactive icons and background differences need enough contrast.
Every tab, including add and profile, can have an active state, and active states are the place to use brand color in a nav bar.
Whether a tab bar needs labels depends on how obscure its icons are; if there are labels, they must be dark enough to read.
Smoothed, curved chart lines hide where the data actually sits; grid lines, markers, a time-frame switcher and a legend make a chart readable.
When cards repeat, the whole card can be the link, with an arrow that fades in on hover; a card with a specific action keeps its button.
A pricing card reads better with a plan name and description, check marks instead of bullets, honest billing text and an actionable button label.
Stickers break out of boxy layouts and are a place to be creative with shape, display fonts, outlines and hard drop shadows.
Labels used as placeholder text disappear while typing; labels belong above the input, and the placeholder should be a real example.
Most sites have 3 to 5 footer links, so a simple centered footer beats copying the many-column footers of Apple or Linear.
Chips differ from buttons: they are thinner vertically and almost never use the primary call-to-action color.
A carousel needs navigation that shows how many images there are and stays visible whatever image is behind it.

topics.name: Mobile app patterns
topics.summary: Redesigns a mobile tab bar: inline add button, visible inactive icons, active states for every tab, a profile picture as the profile tab, wider click areas, optional labels, and an optional dark, translucent, blurred version.

topics.name: Navigation and sidebars
topics.summary: Covers the mobile tab bar, chips used as breadcrumb navigation, a sign-up modal link to log in, and carousel navigation indicators.

topics.name: Dashboards and data display
topics.summary: Fixes a dashboard line chart: horizontal and vertical grid lines, markers, straight rather than curved lines, a time-frame switcher, a gray previous-period line and a legend.

topics.name: Cards and sections
topics.summary: Improves a UI card (text, margins, font, rounded corners), explains when a whole card should be the link, and shows an image card with a smooth gradient overlay and text on top.

topics.name: Paywalls and pricing pages
topics.summary: Rebuilds a pricing card: outline button moved up, check marks instead of bullets, a missing feature listed, a plan name and description, honest billing text, a tinted price area and an actionable button label.

topics.name: Forms and inputs
topics.summary: Sign-up modal fixes: labels above inputs, real example placeholders, a 'create account' subheading, a link to log in, 4 px grid spacing, and an off-white input fill with a 40% opacity stroke.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Chips versus buttons (chips are thinner and rarely the primary color), card links versus explicit calls to action, outline buttons to rebalance hierarchy, and more actionable button labels.

topics.name: Landing pages
topics.summary: Footers: most sites have 3 to 5 links and should use a simple centered layout instead of copying many-column footers.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Argues color differences must have enough contrast to be seen, and that active states are where brand color can add pop in a nav bar; uses a reduced-opacity primary color as a section background.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Moving a pricing button up throws off hierarchy, which is fixed by making it stroke-only; the price area is separated from features with a tinted background.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Adds space to a cramped modal, sticks to a 4 px grid for sign-up and login modals, sets chip vertical padding to half or a quarter of horizontal padding, and spreads tab icons to enlarge click areas.

topics.name: Depth, shadows and borders
topics.summary: Sticker depth from a darker, full-opacity, offset drop shadow; input stroke at 40% opacity; blurred dark backgrounds behind tab bars and carousel navigation.

topics.name: Figma and design tools
topics.summary: Figma recipes: the star tool with 12 points for stickers, a text-on-path plugin for circular text, and Shift+A to wrap chip text in an auto layout frame.

topics.name: Content and microcopy
topics.summary: Plan names and descriptions, honest billing text, an actionable call-to-action, a 'create account' subheading, and real example placeholders in inputs.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: An arrow icon that fades in on hover to show a card is a link, and a carousel indicator that extends into a timer for the current image.

topics.name: Design resources
topics.summary: All nine redesigned elements are offered as a free, editable Figma file.

rules.rule: Do not raise the tab bar's add or create button above the bar in a circle; drop the icon into line with the other tab icons and keep all icons aligned.
rules.why: People use all of the other tabs most of the time, so the one they use least should not stick out.
rules.evidence: let's drop the icon down and get rid of the circle

rules.rule: Keep inactive tab bar icons clearly visible; show the active tab with its own active style instead of fading the other icons out.
rules.why: The active state already shows which tab is selected, so the other icons do not need to be impossible to see.
rules.evidence: we don't need to make the other icons impossible to see

rules.rule: Use background colors that differ enough to be noticed; if two surfaces are meant to look different, give them visible contrast.
rules.why: The whole point of using colors is that people can see them; in the original, nobody could tell the backgrounds were different.
rules.evidence: there are fact different background colors here neither could I

rules.rule: Give every tab an active state, including the add tab, by using an icon that has an active version.
rules.why: Swapping the plus icon for one with an active version lets that tab show when it is selected too.
rules.evidence: we can now have an active state for that too

rules.rule: Use the person's profile picture as the profile tab icon when they have uploaded one.
rules.why: The source suggests swapping the generic user icon for the uploaded profile picture.
rules.evidence: Swap this user icon for a profile picture if they upload one

rules.rule: If you want to add some pop of brand color to a nav bar, use it on the active states.
rules.why: The source says active states are a good place to play around with brand colors if you want to add some pop.
rules.evidence: active states are a good place to play around with your brand colors

rules.rule: Spread tab bar icons a little further apart to enlarge each click area.
rules.why: Shifting the icons out increases the click area.
rules.evidence: shift them out just a bit to increase our click area

rules.rule: If a tab bar has text labels, make them dark enough to read.
rules.why: The source insists on it ('for God's sake'); labels that are too light cannot be read.
rules.evidence: for God's sake make them dark enough to read

rules.rule: Add text labels to a tab bar when its icons are obscure; icon-only tabs suit familiar icons.
rules.why: Whether to label depends on how obscure the icons are: the Instagram app has no labels, while apps like Apple Music do.
rules.evidence: it just depends on how obscure your icons are

rules.rule: On a small chart that cannot be made larger, add horizontal grid lines and data markers.
rules.why: They give the reader some clue of the fluctuations; without them the chart looks good but functionally fails.
rules.evidence: add some horizontal grid lines and some markers

rules.rule: Do not smooth line-chart lines into curves; draw straight segments between data points.
rules.why: The source says the curving needs to be turned off and calls it a bad trend: it makes it very difficult to tell where the tip of the line actually is.
rules.evidence: turn off the curving of these lines this is a bad Trend

rules.rule: Do not fade out or play down the most recent data in a chart [inferred: the caption reads 'the St out', likely a fade-out].
rules.why: It almost makes it seem like we don't want to know what is going on with our money.
rules.evidence: especially of the most recent data almost makes it seem like we don't want to know

rules.rule: When a chart has room, add vertical grid lines so readers can judge the time scale.
rules.why: They give a better sense of the time scale.
rules.evidence: add some vertical chart lines so we can get a better sense of the time scale

rules.rule: Let people switch a chart's time frame: use a dropdown when space is short, otherwise lay the time frames out as separate options.
rules.why: People should have the ability to switch the time frame.
rules.evidence: we can use a drop down if we're short on space

rules.rule: For business metrics such as income or sales, show the previous period as a gray line behind the current one.
rules.why: In the month time frame, the previous month's sales give useful comparison; this is less relevant for a stock portfolio.
rules.evidence: represented by this Gray Line

rules.rule: Include a legend on charts that compare lines, unless the chart is intuitive enough without one.
rules.why: A legend is often nice to include.
rules.evidence: a legend is often nice to include

rules.rule: When a chart is already shown large, remove the button that only opens a larger version of the same chart.
rules.why: The source assumes the button only leads to a bigger copy of the same chart, which is redundant once it is scaled up.
rules.evidence: get rid of this button which I assume takes you to a larger version

rules.rule: Round card corners to give cards a friendlier look.
rules.why: Rounding off the edges helps give everything a more friendly look.
rules.evidence: rounding off the edges also helps to give everything a more friendly look

rules.rule: In a card, fix the image and text margins, make the paragraph text a bit smaller and switch to a more modern font.
rules.why: These are the first fixes the source makes to his old card design, which he calls awful.
rules.evidence: drop the size of the paragraph text a bit and switch everything to a more modern font

rules.rule: When cards repeat over and over, make the whole card the link and drop the call-to-action button.
rules.why: You generally do not need a CTA because the entire card becomes the link.
rules.evidence: you generally don't actually need a CTA

rules.rule: If the whole card is a link, fade in an arrow icon on hover to show it can be clicked.
rules.why: The source says you can make it clear that the card is a link this way.
rules.evidence: having an arrow icon fade in on Hover

rules.rule: Keep an explicit call-to-action button on a card when it has a specific action, such as 'Try it out'.
rules.why: A specific call to action should be included rather than left implicit in the card link.
rules.evidence: if you have a specific call to action like try it out

rules.rule: For an image card with text over the image, make the image about 3/4 of the card height and overlay a gradient that runs smoothly from the bottom of the image up, then place the text on top.
rules.why: The smoother the transition, the better the effect looks.
rules.evidence: start with your image about 3/4 the height of the card

rules.rule: When a pricing card's button moves higher up the card, make it an outline button (stroke only, no fill) to keep the hierarchy.
rules.why: Moving the button up throws off the hierarchy; removing the background and keeping the stroke fixes it.
rules.evidence: removing the background and just having stroke on the button

rules.rule: Use check marks instead of bullet points for a pricing card's feature list.
rules.why: The source replaces bullet points with check marks as part of the upgrade.
rules.evidence: replace them with check marks

rules.rule: Consider listing a feature that the plan does not include.
rules.why: The source adds one 'for good measure' to the plan card.
rules.evidence: add a feature that users don't get with this specific plan

rules.rule: Give each pricing plan a name and a short description.
rules.why: A name makes the plan easier to identify.
rules.evidence: let's give it a name so it's easier to identify and a little description too

rules.rule: Add a short note to the pricing card that states the real billing terms [inferred: its exact position is only shown on screen].
rules.why: So users do not think the company is being dishonest when they find out what they actually pay (the example: it is actually $20 a month).
rules.evidence: our users don't think we're bad people

rules.rule: Separate a pricing card's price area from its feature list with a reduced-opacity tint of the primary color as the background, instead of a divider line.
rules.why: The source wants to separate the numbers from the features, as Hostinger does, and prefers the tint to a literal divider.
rules.evidence: a reduced opacity version of our primary color for the background

rules.rule: Write the pricing card's call to action as a more actionable phrase.
rules.why: The source changes the button label to something more actionable as the final step of the upgrade.
rules.evidence: change the call to action to something a little more actionable

rules.rule: Consider stickers to break out of boxy layouts and add information, and be creative with their shapes, colors and patterns.
rules.why: Stickers break up boxy layouts, and they are where you should try to get very creative.
rules.evidence: these kind of elements are definitely where you should try and get very creative

rules.rule: Make a sticker shape in Figma from the star tool with 12 points, drag out the ratio and round the corners; optionally add an outline or circular text for extra detail.
rules.why: This is the source's recipe for this kind of sticker.
rules.evidence: grab the star tool and add 12 points to it

rules.rule: Use quirky display fonts on stickers.
rules.why: The source likes quirky display fonts for this kind of sticker.
rules.evidence: I like to use quirky display fonts

rules.rule: Give a sticker depth with a hard drop shadow: a darker color than the sticker, at full opacity, offset a little.
rules.why: It adds depth to the sticker.
rules.evidence: drop shadow that's a darker color than our sticker and is at full opacity

rules.rule: Do not use labels as placeholder text inside inputs; put labels above the inputs where they are always visible.
rules.why: The source calls a modal with labels as the empty states awful: if someone gets halfway through typing and forgets what they are typing, the label is gone.
rules.evidence: move them up above the inputs where they're always visible

rules.rule: Fill input placeholders with a realistic example of the expected entry.
rules.why: It lets people see an example before they enter their information.
rules.evidence: allows the user to see an example before they enter their information

rules.rule: Add a subheading such as 'Create account' to a sign-up modal.
rules.why: It makes clear this is a sign-up and not a login.
rules.evidence: so it's clear that this is a sign up and not a login

rules.rule: Give a sign-up modal a small link or button that takes people to log in instead.
rules.why: People who want to log in should be able to navigate there easily.
rules.evidence: so people can easily navigate to log in

rules.rule: Lay out sign-up and login modals on a 4 px grid.
rules.why: The source states it as a rule he always follows religiously for sign-up and login modals, after adding space because the labels made the modal feel cramped.
rules.evidence: I always stick to a 4 pixel grid religiously

rules.rule: Style text inputs with an off-white background and the stroke reduced to 40% opacity.
rules.why: The source adds this to make the input field look nicer.
rules.evidence: add an off-white background and reduce the stroke to a 40% opacity

rules.rule: Do not copy the many-column footer of a large site (such as Apple or Linear) when your site has only a few links.
rules.why: Your website probably does not have that many links, and giant footers look awful with only about six links in them.
rules.evidence: your website probably doesn't have 23 godamn links

rules.rule: For a footer with about 3 to 5 links, center the links, put the logo above them and socials below in the center, with the copyright on the left and design credits on the right.
rules.why: It keeps things simple, avoids five columns of links, and also looks great in dark mode.
rules.evidence: somewhere between 3 to five links which is a pretty normal amount

rules.rule: If a footer needs more than about five links, use a different layout from the simple centered one.
rules.why: The simple centered footer only fits the fiveish links it has room for.
rules.evidence: then you will need to consider a different layout

rules.rule: Do not give chips the primary call-to-action color, and keep them thinner vertically than buttons.
rules.why: That is the difference between chips and buttons; make the chip too large and it becomes a button.
rules.evidence: chips almost never have the primary CTA as their color and are always thinner vertically

rules.rule: Consider chips for breadcrumb navigation and for adding interaction to an experience.
rules.why: The source finds them practical for breadcrumb navigation and says they lend themselves to adding some interaction.
rules.evidence: they're practical for a breadcrumb navigation

rules.rule: Set a chip's vertical padding to half or a quarter of its horizontal padding (for example 20 px horizontal gives 10 px or 5 px vertical).
rules.why: The source's preferred ratio, given right after his warning that a chip background that is too small looks wrong and one that is too large becomes a button.
rules.evidence: vertical padding to be either a half or a quarter of the horizontal padding

rules.rule: Build chips in Figma with auto layout (select the text and press Shift+A), then add the background, round the edges and adjust the padding.
rules.why: The source says to always use auto layout whenever dealing with a chip.
rules.evidence: whenever you're dealing with a chip always use Auto layout

rules.rule: Give a carousel navigation indicators that show how many images there are.
rules.why: Without them people cannot tell how many photos there are.
rules.evidence: adding some navigation so we can tell how many photos there are

rules.rule: Place carousel navigation either on a dark, blurred background over the image or below the image, so it stays readable whatever the image is.
rules.why: Controls placed directly on the image look fine with one image but become unreadable when the image changes.
rules.evidence: put it on a dark background with some blur but you could also put this below the image

rules.rule: Move a carousel's arrows down beside its navigation indicators.
rules.why: The source groups the arrows with the navigation in the upgraded design.
rules.evidence: move them down beside our navigation

rules.rule: Consider extending the active carousel indicator into a timer for the current image.
rules.why: An optional flourish the source calls 'extra fancy'.
rules.evidence: turn it into a timer for the image

decisions.question: Should the tab bar show text labels under its icons?

options.name: Icon only
options.effect: No text under the icons; people must recognise each icon (the Instagram app has no labels).
options.when: When the icons are familiar and not obscure.

options.name: Icons with labels
options.effect: Each tab is named in text under its icon, as in Apple Music; the labels must be dark enough to read.
options.when: When the icons are obscure.

decisions.recommendation: It depends on how obscure the icons are; if labels are used, make them dark enough to read.
decisions.evidence: it just depends on how obscure your icons are

decisions.question: Should the tab bar's add or create button stand out from the other tabs?

options.name: Raised circled button
options.effect: A circle that sticks up above the bar and dominates it.
options.when: The source gives no case where this is right; it only notes that the idea is to push people to add content.

options.name: Inline icon with an active state
options.effect: The add icon sits in line with the others and gets its own active state like every other tab.
options.when: By default.

decisions.recommendation: Inline icon with an active state, because people use the other tabs most of the time.
decisions.evidence: button that sticks up like a sore thumb

decisions.question: Should the tab bar be solid, or dark with transparency and blur?

options.name: Solid bar
options.effect: An opaque bar with clear contrast between icons and background.
options.when: The default in the redesign.

options.name: Dark mode with transparency and blur
options.effect: The content behind shows through a blurred, dark, see-through bar, which looks a little fancier.
options.when: When applying the redesign back onto the original design, or to get a little fancy.

decisions.evidence: add some transparency and blur if we wanted to get a little fancy

decisions.question: Should line charts draw smooth curves or straight lines between data points?

options.name: Curved lines
options.effect: A soft, flowing line that hides where each value actually sits.
options.when: The source calls this a bad trend.

options.name: Straight lines
options.effect: Sharp segments that show exactly where each point and the tip of the line are.
options.when: By default.

decisions.recommendation: Straight lines, because curves make it very difficult to tell where the tip of the line actually is.
decisions.evidence: turn off the curving of these lines

decisions.question: How should people switch a chart's time frame?

options.name: Dropdown
options.effect: One compact control that hides the other time frames until opened.
options.when: When you are short on space.

options.name: Separate options laid out side by side
options.effect: All time frames are visible and one click away.
options.when: When there is room.

decisions.evidence: we can use a drop down if we're short on space

decisions.question: Should a chart include a legend?

options.name: Legend
options.effect: A key explains each line, such as the gray previous-period line.
options.when: Often nice to include.

options.name: No legend
options.effect: Less clutter, relying on the reader to understand the lines.
options.when: When the chart is intuitive enough.

decisions.recommendation: A legend is often nice to include.
decisions.evidence: a legend is often nice to include

decisions.question: Should a card have its own call-to-action button, or should the whole card be the link?

options.name: Whole card is the link
options.effect: No button; an arrow icon fades in on hover to show the card is clickable.
options.when: When many cards repeat over and over.

options.name: Explicit call-to-action button
options.effect: A visible button such as 'Try it out' on the card.
options.when: When the card has a specific call to action.

decisions.recommendation: Whole-card link for repeated cards; keep the button when there is a specific action.
decisions.evidence: if you have many cards repeating over and over

decisions.question: Should card text sit beside or below the image, or on top of it with a gradient?

options.name: Standard card
options.effect: Image and text in separate areas of the card; it always works.
options.when: When the images and colors vary or are unknown.

options.name: Image with a gradient overlay
options.effect: The image fills about 3/4 of the card and a smooth gradient carries the text on top, as on some Apple Music albums.
options.when: Only with some images and colors.

decisions.recommendation: The source leaves it to taste but notes the overlay card only works with some images and colors, while the standard card always works.
decisions.evidence: the card on the right will only work with some images and colors

decisions.question: How should a pricing card separate the price from the feature list?

options.name: Divider line
options.effect: A literal line between the two areas.
options.when: Not stated.

options.name: Tinted price area
options.effect: The price area sits on a reduced-opacity version of the primary color, as Hostinger does.
options.when: The source's choice.

decisions.recommendation: A reduced-opacity tint of the primary color instead of a literal divider.
decisions.evidence: We could use a literal divider but instead

decisions.question: Where should form field labels go?

options.name: Label as placeholder inside the input
options.effect: Does not look terrible, but the label is gone once someone starts typing.
options.when: The source calls this awful even though it does not look terrible.

options.name: Label above the input
options.effect: The label is always visible, and the placeholder can show a real example.
options.when: By default.

decisions.recommendation: Labels above the inputs, with real example placeholders inside.
decisions.evidence: move them up above the inputs where they're always visible

decisions.question: What kind of footer should the site have?

options.name: Many-column footer
options.effect: Several columns of links, like the footers of Apple or Linear, which look awful with only about six links.
options.when: The source only says that more than about five links needs a different layout; it does not name which.

options.name: Simple centered footer
options.effect: Logo above centered links, socials below, copyright on the left and design credits on the right; it also works in dark mode.
options.when: When there are about 3 to 5 links, a pretty normal amount.

decisions.recommendation: The simple centered footer for most sites, which do not need giant footers.
decisions.evidence: let's make something that looks simple and elegant

decisions.question: How much vertical padding should a chip have?

options.name: Half the horizontal padding
options.effect: A slightly taller chip (20 px horizontal gives 10 px vertical).
options.when: Not distinguished by the source.

options.name: A quarter of the horizontal padding
options.effect: A thinner, tighter chip (20 px horizontal gives 5 px vertical).
options.when: Not distinguished by the source.

decisions.recommendation: Either half or a quarter; the chip must stay thinner than a button.
decisions.evidence: this can either be 10 pixels or five

decisions.question: Where should a carousel's navigation sit?

options.name: Over the image on a dark, blurred background
options.effect: Indicators and arrows sit on a dark, blurred background over the photo and stay readable on any image.
options.when: The source's 'fancy' choice.

options.name: Below the image
options.effect: Navigation sits under the photo, so the image never interferes with it.
options.when: Also offered as an option.

process.step: Audit borrowed elements for UI and UX
process.detail: When taking an element from a showcase like Dribbble, check how it works as well as how it looks: contrast, active states, click areas, labels and whether its data or controls can actually be read.

Drop the raised add button into line, align the icons, raise contrast of inactive icons, give every tab an active state (swap the plus icon, use the profile picture), use brand color on active states, spread icons to enlarge click areas, decide on labels, and optionally make a dark, translucent, blurred version.

Add horizontal grid lines and markers, straighten curved lines; if the chart can be larger, move the title, remove the 'open larger' button, add vertical grid lines, add time-frame options (a dropdown if space is short), add a gray previous-period line for business data, and add a legend.

Rewrite the text, fix the image and text margins, make the paragraph text a bit smaller, switch to a more modern font, round the corners, then decide between a whole-card link (with a hover arrow) and an explicit call-to-action button.
Make the image about 3/4 of the card height, overlay a smooth gradient that stretches from the bottom of the image upward, then place the text on top.

Move the button up and make it stroke-only, use check marks for features, list a feature the plan lacks, add a plan name and description, add honest billing text, tint the price area with a reduced-opacity primary color, and make the button label actionable.

Use the star tool with 12 points, drag out the ratio, round the corners, set a quirky display font, optionally add an outline or circular text (via a text-on-path plugin), and add a darker, full-opacity, slightly offset drop shadow.

Move labels above the inputs, put real examples in the placeholders, add a 'create account' subheading, add a link to log in, add space on a 4 px grid, then give inputs an off-white fill and a 40% opacity stroke; reuse the layout for login.

For 3 to 5 links: center the links, put the logo above them, socials below in the center, the copyright on the left and the design credits on the right; use a different layout only if you need more than about five links.
Type the chip text, press Shift+A to wrap it in an auto layout frame, add a background, round the edges, then set vertical padding to half or a quarter of the horizontal padding.

Add indicators showing how many images there are, put them on a dark blurred background (or below the image), move the arrows beside them, and optionally turn the active indicator into a timer; the source shows it working on desktop and mobile.

caveats: Self-promotion: the video offers the nine elements as a free Figma file (link in the description), asks viewers to subscribe, and points to a separate video on the kaleidoscope effect.
The redesigns are the creator's opinion and taste (he asks 'which one do you like more'); few rules are backed by data or cited sources.
Positions shown on screen are not in the transcript ('drag this button up here', 'up to about here'), so exact placements such as where the pricing button moves are not known from the text.

Auto-caption errors: 'the St out' of the most recent chart data is garbled (likely a fade-out, but not certain); the sticker display fonts appear as 'gourd quick or barito' and the plugin as 'two path', neither of which could be confirmed; the chip example site appears as 'Linder'.
Several steps are Figma-specific (star tool, Shift+A for auto layout, a text-on-path plugin) and describe Figma as of June 2024.
No media list exists for this video, so no images were reviewed; examples are described from the transcript only.
